newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission offers TV programmes cash to promote EU ideas.
newsitem.headline: Commission offers TV programmes cash to promote EU ideas.

text.p: The European Commission, seeking a better public understanding of the European Union's single currency and closer integration plans, will on Tuesday offer the bloc's television programmers cash to put the message across.

At a meeting with around 60 public and private television producers the Commission will encourage them to stage debates and documentaries about the EU's plans to fight an ignorance which it feels fuels Euroscepticism.

"What they are going to tell the television producers in Europe is...listen, we have this money available," said a spokesman for the EU's Culture Commissioner Marcelino Oreja, referring to 20 million Ecus available for EU information campaigns.

"If you present a programme on the Euro, or spread the idea, probably we can finance this to help to produce in television this campaign (to promote the euro, the single market and the inter-governmental conference review of the Mastricht Treaty)," he said
Last week in Portugal Yves-Thibault de Silguy, the Comissioner responsible for the single currency, said the EU must do a better job to explain to its citizens why they would benefit from it.
"The main problem today is the lack of information available to European citizens," said de Silguy, adding "80 to 90 percent of Europeans consider themselves badly informed about the Euro."
Polls indicate that the British have turned sharply against the European Union while the vast majority of Germans want a referendum on a single currency.

In Britain -- completely separately from the EU campaign -- the respected British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) television news programme Panorama prepared to stage a special "Euro debate" later on Monday, saying British voters felt they had not got enough information about what they considered to be a key election issue.

A survey of more than 1,500 people prepared for the programme said 65 percent felt poorly informed and 34 percent well informed about the Euro. More than half of those interviewed opposed the currency.

A spokesman for the programme, asked how the programmers would have reacted to the offer of EU money to fund the programme, said accepting EU cash would not necessarily conflict with the aim of objective programming.
"The programmers should maintain their integrity and journalistic independence wherever the money is coming from," he said.

The EU campaign, prepared by the Commission's information directorate, seeks to dispel strong criticism from the European Parliament that the Commission has not carried out campaigns on the Euro, the single market and the IGC well enough.
German Euro-deputy Detlev Samland, one of the Commission's strongest critics, told Reuters the campaign seemed to be going in the right direction.
Among the broadcasters who will be attending the Brussels meeting are the BBC, the French television channels France 2 and FR3, Germany's ARD and Belgium's RTBF and BRT.
